items.topic: Weather Derivatives: Purpose and Volumetric Risk
items.definition: Weather derivatives are financial contracts whose payout is determined by measured weather outcomes (such as average temperature or rainfall) rather than by the price or delivery of a commodity.
items.core_idea: Utilities and insurers use weather derivatives to hedge volumetric risk — the tendency for customers to consume more of an energy product exactly when prices are high and less when prices are low, which forces the utility to buy extra supply at expensive prices and unload surplus supply cheaply.
key_points: Payoff is linked to a weather index, most commonly average temperature, but also rainfall, snowfall, or hurricane data
Contracts are typically bilaterally negotiated between counterparties seeking protection from, or exposure to, a weather outcome
Typical users are utilities and insurance companies

Weather creates a combined volume-and-price risk that ordinary financial hedges struggle to address: an unusually cold winter both drains gas storage (more heating demand) and pushes gas prices higher as utilities compete for dwindling reserves
relationships: Weather derivatives are distinct from price hedges because weather affects both consumption volume and price simultaneously
trading_implications: A pure price hedge (e.g., a gas swap) does not protect a utility against volumetric risk, so weather derivatives fill a separate hedging need
common_misunderstandings: Weather risk is not simply a price risk; it is a coupled volume-and-price risk that standard commodity derivatives don't fully cover

items.definition: A comparison of how weather derivatives differ from traditional insurance products despite serving a similar protective purpose.
items.core_idea: Weather derivatives are designed for higher-probability, less extreme outcomes than insurance, which is built for rare, catastrophic losses.
key_points: Weather derivatives tend to cover events with a reasonably high probability of occurring

Weather derivatives tend to cover less extreme events than insurance — e.g., insurance might cover a flood or hurricane loss expected roughly once every 100 years, while a weather derivative might cover a smaller loss (like rainfall 10% above average) that could recur several times within a 10-year span
relationships: Weather derivatives and insurance both transfer weather-related loss risk, but differ in the probability and severity of the covered event
common_misunderstandings: Weather derivatives should not be assumed to function like catastrophe insurance — they target frequent, moderate deviations, not rare disasters

items.topic: Weather Derivative Structures: Swap vs. Option
items.definition: The two contractual forms weather derivatives commonly take, each with a different risk and payment profile.
items.core_idea: A weather swap puts both counterparties at risk with no upfront payment, while a weather option requires the buyer to pay a premium so that only the seller bears risk; premiums on weather options tend to be large relative to the payout, and many contracts cap the maximum gain or loss.
key_points: In a swap, both parties are at risk and there is no cost to enter the contract
In an option, the buyer pays a premium to the seller and only the seller is at risk
The option premium is typically quite large — often around 20 percent of the maximum payout
It is fairly common for weather derivatives to cap the maximum profit or loss
relationships: Swap/option structure mirrors other derivative types but with unusually high premium-to-payout ratios for options
trading_implications: The high premium (~20% of max payout) reflects the difficulty of precisely modeling weather outcomes and should be weighed against the capped payout when evaluating option economics
common_misunderstandings: Unlike many financial options where premiums are a small fraction of notional exposure, weather option premiums are proportionally large

items.topic: Heating Degree Days (HDD) and Cooling Degree Days (CDD)
items.definition: HDD and CDD are daily measures of how far the average temperature deviates from a reference baseline, used as the underlying index for most weather derivatives.
items.core_idea: HDDs accumulate on cold days when heating is needed (temperature below baseline), and CDDs accumulate on hot days when cooling is needed (temperature above baseline); the daily values are summed over a contract period and compared to a strike to determine payoff.
key_points: HDD and CDD contracts are the most common form of weather derivative
Common baseline temperatures are 65°F in the United States and 18°C in Europe
Example: an 85°F average daily temperature against a 65°F baseline contributes 20 CDD
Daily HDD/CDD values are accumulated over the contract period and compared against a strike to compute the payoff

variables.Average Temperature: observed daily average temperature at the reference station
observed daily average temperature at the reference station

relationships: HDD/CDD accumulated over a period is compared to a contract Strike to compute the payoff of an HDD/CDD weather derivative
trading_implications: Payoff sensitivity depends on the chosen baseline and reference weather station, both of which are specified in the contract

items.topic: Worked Example: HDD Contract Payoff Calculation
items.definition: An illustrative walk-through of how an HDD contract's payoff is derived from daily temperature observations.
items.core_idea: For a contract paying, say, $1,000 per HDD above a 100 HDD strike for a given week, the calculation requires: obtaining each day's average temperature from the contractually specified official source and location, converting each day into an HDD using the contract's baseline, and summing the daily HDDs across the period before comparing to the strike.
key_points: The contract specifies the official weather data source, the location, and the baseline temperature used for the HDD calculation
An HDD is generated for each degree the daily average temperature falls below the baseline
The period (e.g., weekly) HDD total is the sum of the daily HDD values
The accumulated HDD is then compared against the contract's strike to determine the payoff
relationships: Applies the HDD formula from 'Heating Degree Days (HDD) and Cooling Degree Days (CDD)' over a defined period
trading_implications: Accurate payoff estimation requires knowing the exact reference station, baseline, and period defined in the trade confirmation, not just a general HDD formula

items.topic: Standard Terms in a Weather Derivative Confirmation
items.definition: A glossary of the standard fields found in a weather derivative trade confirmation, analogous to confirmations for other derivatives traded under master netting agreements.
items.core_idea: A weather derivative confirmation documents the parties, key dates, the weather index and station(s) used, the baseline/strike/notional mechanics, the payoff formula, and the maximum payment amounts, mirroring the structured documentation used for other OTC derivatives.
key_points: Buyer/Seller: in an option, the buyer pays the premium and the seller receives it; in a swap, the parties may not be labeled buyer/seller and their responsibilities are described directly
Trade Date: the date the parties agreed to the transaction; Effective Date: when payoff calculations begin; Termination Date: when payoff calculations end
HDD Reference Level: the baseline temperature used for the HDD calculation
Strike: the quantity of HDD compared against the accumulated HDD to determine payoff
Notional Amount: a monetary quantity multiplied by a contract-defined factor to compute payoff, e.g. Payoff = (Notional Amount) × Max(Strike – Accumulated HDD, 0)
Maximum Transaction Payment Amount: caps the total money at risk (e.g., limits what the seller must pay the buyer in an option); swaps can cap exposure for both sides
Premium and Premium Payment Date: the amount the buyer pays the seller to enter the trade (often zero in a swap) and when it is due
Reference Weather Station: the station(s) whose observations define the weather index; if multiple stations are used, the contract specifies the combination method (e.g., a weighted average)
Weather Index Unit: describes the underlying weather commodity/measure the derivative is based on
Transaction Type: a high-level description of the trade for the reader, with full detail spelled out elsewhere in the contract

variables.Notional Amount: monetary multiplier defined in the contract
variables.Accumulated HDD: sum of daily HDD over the contract period

relationships: These terms collectively define how the HDD/CDD formulas in the contract translate into an actual cash payoff
trading_implications: Reviewing all of these fields (not just the strike and notional) is necessary to fully understand a weather derivative's risk exposure, since caps and station definitions materially affect payout
common_misunderstandings: The 'Transaction Type' field is only a high-level summary for convenience; the binding terms are elsewhere in the contract
related_topics: Heating Degree Days (HDD) and Cooling Degree Days (CDD)

items.topic: Valuing Weather Derivatives from Historical Data
items.definition: Unlike most forward prices, which are set by trading markets (nonstorable products) or cost-of-carry/storage (storable products), the pre-expiration expected payoff of a weather derivative is typically estimated from historical weather observations.
items.core_idea: Because weather data tend to trend over time rather than reliably reverting to a stable average, it is difficult to define a single reliable 'expected temperature' for pricing a weather derivative ahead of expiration.
key_points: Most forward commodity prices come from active trading markets (nonstorable energy products) or from buying-and-storing economics (stocks, bonds, storable commodities)
Weather derivative valuation instead relies on analyzing historical weather data since there is no equivalent traded forward market for weather itself
Historical weather data appears to trend rather than consistently revert to an expected value
This trending behavior makes it hard to specify a dependable 'expected temperature' for the following year
relationships: Contrasts weather derivative valuation with standard forward-pricing methods used elsewhere in energy trading
trading_implications: Pricing models that assume mean-reverting historical averages may misstate expected weather derivative payoffs given the observed trending behavior of weather data
common_misunderstandings: It is tempting to assume a long-run historical average temperature is a reliable proxy for next year's expected temperature, but the source notes weather data does not consistently revert to such an average
related_topics: Heating Degree Days (HDD) and Cooling Degree Days (CDD)
